subject: chemistry

moments.title: Perkin tries to make quinine
moments.who: William Henry Perkin, Royal College of Chemistry, London
moments.body:
William Perkin is an 18-year-old chemistry student in August Wilhelm von Hofmann's lab. Hofmann had speculated about synthesising quinine (the antimalarial extracted from cinchona bark) from coal tar derivatives.

Over the Easter holiday, Perkin works in his home laboratory (a board over the bath). He oxidises aniline (a coal-tar derivative) with potassium dichromate. He gets a black tarry sludge. Washing it with alcohol gives a brilliant purple solution.

He has not made quinine. He has made the first synthetic organic dye — mauveine.
moments.takeaway: A failed undergraduate synthesis produces a new dye. Industrial chemistry has its founding accident.

moments.title: Perkin files a patent and builds a factory
moments.body:
Perkin (still 18, technically a minor) recognises the commercial potential. He files a patent in August 1856. With his father and brother, he sets up the first synthetic dyestuffs factory at Greenford, just west of London.

The dye is launched as 'Tyrian purple', then renamed 'mauve' after the French for the mallow flower. Queen Victoria wears mauve to her daughter's wedding in 1858. The colour explodes across European fashion.
moments.takeaway: A teenager builds a chemical industry from scratch using a serendipitous result.

moments.title: German synthetic dye industry overtakes Britain
moments.body:
German chemists and industrialists build on Perkin's discovery far more systematically. By the 1880s, BASF, Hoechst, Bayer and Agfa dominate synthetic dye production worldwide.

The research tradition spreads from dyes to pharmaceuticals: aspirin (Bayer 1899), Salvarsan (Ehrlich 1909, the first chemotherapeutic for syphilis), Prontosil (the first sulfa antibiotic, 1932) all come from the dye-research culture.
moments.takeaway: Industrial chemistry concentrates in Germany. By 1900, German organic chemistry dominates the world.

moments.title: Perkin's 50th anniversary celebration
moments.who: Society of Chemical Industry, London and New York
moments.body:
Perkin is honoured worldwide. He receives the first Perkin Medal in 1906 (still awarded annually in the United States) and is knighted by King Edward VII in 1906. He dies in 1907.

His Greenford factory site is now a residential estate; a blue plaque marks his discovery's role.
moments.takeaway: An accidental discovery created a multibillion-pound industry over a single human lifetime.

now.title: Synthetic dyes and downstream chemistry today
now.body:
Synthetic dyes — and the broader synthetic chemistry tradition they founded — underpin pharmaceuticals, plastics, photography, agrochemicals and modern colour printing. The IUPAC Colour Index lists thousands of synthetic dyes.

Mauveine itself has long been replaced by cheaper and more colourfast purples (notably methyl violet and similar triphenylmethane dyes). But the chemistry tradition Perkin started endures.
now.open_questions: Can chemistry replace petroleum-based dye precursors with sustainable bio-based feedstocks? Can dye chemistry be redirected to functional materials (OLED emitters, dye-sensitised solar cells, photodynamic therapy agents)?

reflection: Perkin retired wealthy at 36 to focus on pure research. His 'failure' to make quinine gave him a fortune and gave the world a colour-and-pharma industry. How should we judge scientific failures that turn out to be more important than the goals they failed at?
